content: These are four stories that seem unrelated: 1) The bond markets are collapsing; 2) Ninety percent of Americans believe that the government is corrupt; 3) Bernie Sanders wants to jail you for 20 years if you develop AI any further; and 4) Russia is prodding NATO and China is prodding Japan. But all four are part of the same big story. Nobody else in American politics will tell you this, so I’m going to. There is, in fact, a uniparty. That uniparty is hell-bent on bankrupting the country, all in the name of populism. Empires don’t die. Empires generally commit suicide, and in the same way: by spending too much money. They may spend too much money in different ways, but they all die the same way: they run out of money. Here in the United States, we spent the money, and then we spent more of the money, and now we are spending all the money for the rest of time. That brings us to our first story. Our bond markets are in a state of total disarray right now. As PBS reports: Interest rates on government bonds are rising again around the world, making borrowing more expensive for consumers and businesses and heightening concerns about whether governments are issuing more debt than financial markets can handle. On Tuesday, the yield on the ten year Treasury, which strongly influences mortgage rates, reached 4.8%. That’s the highest since early 2025. The five-year Treasury, which is a benchmark for auto loans, touched as high as level since October 2025 at 4.55%. For those who don’t know, the way that the bond markets work goes like this: You buy a bond. The bond returns 10% year on year — which would be an amazing bond, but we are keeping the math simple here — you pay $100 for the bond; every year you receive $10. So the bond yield is the difference between the price that you paid for the bond and what you receive for the bond, and that’s what the yield is. Typically, the yield is a measure of the return you receive relative to the price you paid. When we say that bond yields are rising, we mean typically that the price for bonds is falling, meaning that there’s not a lot of demand for bonds, and you are paying a lower price for bonds. The facial rate of interest is exactly the same. What does that actually mean? It means there’s no market for bonds; people don’t want to buy bonds. Sometimes that’s happening because people would rather invest in the stock market because it is soaring. Sometimes it means people don’t want to buy bonds because they are very nervous that anyone will ever be able to pay them off, except in inflated currency. The latter scenario seems to be happening right now, and this is having some broad spillover effect in the American economy. Mortgage rates have now hit their highest level in over a year. content: More than a century ago, American families could flip through a Sears, Roebuck and Co. catalog, pick out a house, and have nearly everything they needed to build it delivered to them at an affordable price. Tens of thousands of Sears homes are still standing today – a testament to an era when a starter home could be both attainable and built to last. Today, as more Americans are priced out of the housing market, Groundwork Collaborative released a new proposal to revive the Sears home model for the 21st century. The Modern Sears Home: Resurrecting the Affordable American Starter Home for a New Generation, authored by Groundwork’s Noah Ball-Burack, Emily DiVito, and Alex Jacquez, outlines a federal initiative to deliver, over eight years, 500,000 high-quality factory-built homes directly to American families across the country for under $215,000. Today, the national median home price hovers above $400,000, and the starter home – what used to be the first rung on the ladder to economic security – is all but extinct . In some communities, starter homes can cost $1 million or more, putting homeownership further out of reach for many families. The Modern Sears Home Program would deploy the federal government’s purchasing power, land access, and ability to finance and site homes at scale to bring the cost of new, high-quality homes within reach. Furthermore, by guaranteeing demand for hundreds of thousands of factory-built homes, the program would also give private manufacturing firms the certainty they need to expand production, lower production costs, and increase housing supply. By bringing affordable homes directly to communities where the private market has fallen short, the Modern Sears Home Program could expand homeownership in rural areas and open the door for families who have historically been shut out of the housing market. The idea has vast public support. New polling shows that three in four voters support the Modern Sears Home Program and the proposal enjoys broad support across party lines, including 80% of Democrats, 72% of Independents, and 74% of Republicans. Additionally, 69% of voters, including majorities across party lines, say the program would make homeownership feel more attainable. By some estimates, Sears sold more than 70,000 catalog kit homes during the 20th century, many of which are still standing today in states like Ohio, Illinois, New York, Michigan and Pennsylvania. Groundwork’s Senior Advisor for Economic Policy, Emily DiVito , shared the following: “For too many families, homeownership has gone from a milestone to a mirage. Decades of under-building have left us with an affordable housing shortage that’s pricing people out of their communities. Policymakers must pursue creative, tangible, and lasting solutions that bring homeownership back into reach. The Modern Sears Home program does just that.” Lindsay Owens , President and CEO of Groundwork, reacted: “I grew up in a Sears Home, and I know the comfort and stabili
title: The Sears Home Reimagined: A Plan to Deliver 500,000 Affordable, Move-In Ready Starter Homes to Working Families
author: Newswire Editor

content: Our nation’s population is aging, and our housing supply is not ready to meet its evolving needs. According to the U.S. Census Bureau , the number of adults age 65 and over rose by 17 million between 2015 and 2025, growing as a share of the total population from 15% to 19%. By 2030, this share will be 21%. Eighty percent of Americans age 65 and over want to remain in their current homes for as long as possible, but there is an acute shortage of affordable, safe, and accessible homes that allow older adults to age in place. Rising costs for housing, health care, food, and other necessities have left many older adults cash-strapped, with an unprecedented 1 in 3 adults age 65 and up spending more than 30% of their income on housing alone and a growing number experiencing homelessness . An aging housing stock means more homes with deferred maintenance, and most housing units lack baseline accessibility features, as shown below. Share of All Households with Accessibility Features Share of All Households with Accessibility Features (%) Bathroom on entry level: 58%. Bedroom on entry level: 46%. Bedroom and bathroom on entry level: 44%. Ramps, chairlift, stairlift, or platform lift: 6%. Source: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, U.S. Census Bureau, 2019 American Housing Survey Aging in an unsuitable home is dangerous. Deferred repairs and maintenance can lead to problems—from pest infestations and structural defects to substandard electrical and plumbing systems—that pose health hazards , including respiratory illness, lead and carbon monoxide exposure, and physical injury. A lack of home accessibility features also increases the risk of injury including falls , which alone affect a staggering 1 in 4 older adults annually, resulting in over 40,000 deaths, 3.5 million emergency department visits, 1 million hospital stays, and $80 billion in total health care costs. While there are federal and state programs that help older adults weather housing-related costs—including programs for home modification and repair, property tax relief, and utility assistance—they fall far short of the current need. The 21 st Century ROAD to Housing Act , while not targeted specifically toward the housing needs of older Americans, could make aging-friendly housing more plentiful and affordable in five main ways. Broadens access to home repair and accessibility modifications The Act supports home repair and accessibility upgrades in two main ways: Section 202 , the Whole-Home Repairs Act, authorizes a pilot program that—if funded—lets the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) select between two and 10 state, local, tribal, and territorial governments each year for grant awards. This funding will then be distributed as grants to eligible homeowners and as loans to small landlords for home repairs, modifications, and upgrades, which must address one of the following: accessibility (such as grab bars or ramps); basic habitability and safety (such as plum
title: What 21st Century ROAD Means for Older Americans
author: Laura Hausman

content: On May 21, the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Terwilliger Center for Housing Policy held a virtual event to release a report, Homelessness, Housing Markets, and Federal Policy: Local Lessons and Policy Implications. The event coincided with the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) release of its 2025 Point-in-Time (PIT) count, which found that 745,652 people experienced homelessness on a single night in January 2025—down 3% from 2024, but more than 30% higher than a decade prior. The PIT count shows that homelessness remains a pressing national challenge and underscores the need for federal policymakers to learn from effective local strategies for addressing homelessness. The event featured a presentation of the report’s key findings, opening remarks from Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR), and a moderated panel discussion with practitioners and thought leaders at the intersection of homelessness and housing policy. This blog highlights takeaways from the event, which could inform federal policymaking to address homelessness and increase access to affordable housing. The full recording of the event is available on BPC’s website. Coordinated Response Systems and Strong Data Collection Can Drive Reductions in Homelessness Steven Howell, director of operations at the Chattanooga Regional Homeless Coalition, described how his city achieved measurable reductions in homelessness at a time when much of the nation was moving in the opposite direction. Chattanooga invested in system infrastructure, breaking down silos separating agencies to build a coordinated system. This system is based on close cross-agency collaboration, a by-name list of people experiencing homelessness updated daily, and a shared assessment tool used by nearly 40 organizations. Howell described how robust real-time data collection allowed the Coalition to make a compelling case for local government investment in targeted approaches for specific subpopulations. Where policymakers once perceived homelessness as a single abstract condition, the Coalition can now use data to track trends for specific subpopulations—such as youth, families, and veterans—and design tailored interventions. A coordinated system buttressed by strong data collection can unlock targeted local investment and drive measurable progress. Solving Homelessness Requires Addressing Upstream Drivers Sarah Dickmeyer, external affairs manager at Plymouth Housing, explained why homelessness is rising regionally even as Plymouth Housing and its partners in King County, WA, are housing more people than ever. Plymouth provides permanent supportive housing (PSH), pairing long-term affordable housing with supportive services. Dickmeyer explained that PSH is highly effective for people experiencing chronic homelessness but does not address the upstream drivers that push people into homelessness in the first place. title: Four Lessons for Federal Policymakers Drawn from Local Homelessness Strategies
author: Laura Hausman

content: The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) released its latest Point-in-Time (PIT) count , finding that 745,652 people experienced homelessness on a single night in January of 2025. This figure is the first year-over-year decline since 2016 and roughly 3% lower than the 2024 count (771,480)—the highest number on record since HUD standardized its PIT count methodology in 2007. Beneath this top-line number, the national picture on homelessness is more complicated: individual and chronic homelessness hit record highs in 2025, homelessness among those 65 and older continued to rise, and 28 states saw an overall increase in homelessness. The net national year-over-year decrease was largely driven by trends in just two states. This blog answers key questions about the 2025 PIT count. What Drove the Overall Decline in Homelessness? The decrease in homelessness in 2025 is largely attributable to trends in New York and Illinois, where 23,800 fewer people experienced homelessness than in 2024. The reduction in these two states alone accounts for more than 90% of the gross national decrease reflected in the 2025 PIT count. New York and Illinois experienced large increases in homelessness in 2024, likely related to an influx of asylum seekers straining shelter systems in New York City and Chicago. The 2025 decline in homelessness in these two states is best understood as progress toward reversing the 2024 spike. This progress has been incremental and uneven: Illinois reversed roughly 80% of its 2024 influx, while New York has walked back less than 25% of its surge. Homelessness is also rising outside of major cities: suburban Continuums of Care (CoCs) saw a roughly 2% increase in homelessness and 28 states reported higher overall counts than in 2024. How Have Chronic and Individual Homelessness Changed? Chronic homelessness , defined as prolonged or repeated periods of homelessness with a co-occurring disabling condition, rose to a record-high 155,750 people in 2025, a 2% increase from 2024 and a nearly 90% increase since 2015 . One in three homeless individuals is now chronically homeless. While the number of permanent supportive housing beds for chronically homeless individuals rose by 8% in 2025, demand continues to outpace capacity.  Unsheltered chronic homelessness declined by 3%, the first such decrease since 2018 , suggesting that outreach and encampment resolution efforts are beginning to move some of the most entrenched cases indoors. The number of homeless individuals—those not in families—reached a record high of 515,286 in 2025. This group comprises more than 90% of those experiencing chronic homelessness. How Has Family Homelessness Changed? The 2025 PIT count is encouraging with respect to homelessness among families with children, showing an 11% decrease. Part of this decrease is a reversal of the 39% surge in family homelessness in 2024. This surge is likely attributable to several factors, including the expiration of pandemic
title: What Does HUD’s 2025 Point-in-Time Count Tell Us?
author: Laura Hausman

content: America’s older adults are a growing share of the population, but the systems meant to support them haven’t kept up. Older adults and their families struggle to access essential services and barriers hit hardest for select populations, such as people with disabilities, individuals with low incomes, veterans, and rural communities. Policymakers have taken steps to strengthen the nation’s aging system, which provides services to millions of older adults, people with disabilities, and family caregivers. However, progress has been slow, and the existing challenges are worsening as the baby boomer generation ages. Continued inaction will leave Americans without the supports they need to age with dignity, harming older adults and their families while driving up avoidable federal and state costs. The Older Americans Act is a core federal law addressing aging. Congress last reauthorized the law in 2020, with funding authorized through 2024. Congress has since funded the programs at the 2024 levels through continuing resolutions. Most recently, the Senate unanimously passed its version of an extension, the Older Americans Act Reauthorization Act of 2025 . The House has not yet considered the reauthorizing legislation. Through our Aging of America Initiative: Forging a National Consensus for 2029 , the Bipartisan Policy Center is identifying policy recommendations that lower everyday costs and enhance support for older adults and caregivers, strengthen retirement security, and ensure the long-term sustainability of key programs. As policymakers work to close these persistent gaps, understanding the shifting policy landscape is essential to building durable, bipartisan solutions. This article highlights select emerging policy changes BPC is monitoring across three persisting challenges: 1) long-term care, 2) housing, and 3) nutrition . Join BPC’s webinar on July 28 from 1 to 2 p.m. ET to hear from leading experts on these challenges, including the evolving policy landscape and evidence-based solutions to help Americans age with dignity. 1. How is the Long-Term Care System Not Meeting the Needs of Older Adults, People with Disabilities, and Their Families? With the population over 85 projected to almost double from 7 million to nearly 14 million from 2025 to 2040, demand for long-term care will keep rising. When people cannot access the long-term care they need, their health and independence suffer and the strain on family caregivers grows. Medicare generally does not cover long-term care, and complex market challenges have put private insurance out of reach for many.  Millions are forced to spend down their personal net worth to become eligible for Medicaid, which covers long-term care. Many also choose to rely on unpaid family caregivers, a substantial number of whom risk their own financial security by reducing their work hours or leaving the workforce entirely.
